results.title: LoupeKit: See what any page is built with and how much of it is AI
results.content:
1. A 0-100 score across five weighted categories — markup, CSS, runtime, copy, accessibility  
2. 66 heuristics, each finding saying exactly what it measured and what to change  
3. Click a finding and the page scrolls to that element and selects it — you look at the thing, not at a line number  
  
That third one is what I actually wanted. A number on its own is an opinion. A number that walks you to the element it is talking  
about is a review.  
  
The hard part was calibration, in the direction nobody expects: getting it to leave careful hand-written work alone. A tool that  
flags good code is worse than no tool — you stop reading it, and then it never catches the real thing either. [...] One decision I would defend loudest: no website permission at install. Empty host\_permissions in both builds. It reads the tab you  
are on, when you click, and nothing in the background.  
  
Free tier is 3 audits, everything else unlimited. Chrome, Edge, Firefox and others.  
  
Enjoy!  
— Jan [...] LoupeKit

results.title: 😸 Touch Bars, page grades, pull requests | Product Hunt
results.content:
Agent Mode on Arena now integrates directly with GitHub, so you connect a repo in the browser, hand the agent a task, and it creates the pull request, shows you the diff, pushes the commits and merges the change without you leaving the tab. Whatever it writes runs in a disposable cloud environment rather than on your machine, and you can run several at a time. Cursor gave up on GitHub for exactly this last week and built its own, so the two of them are now pulling in opposite directions on the same problem.

LoupeKit — See what any page is built with and how much of it is AI [...] LoupeKit is basically a second opinion for whatever’s happening under the hood of a webpage. The browser extension identifies the tech stack, then grades the page across markup, CSS, runtime, copy and accessibility using 66 checks. The nice bit: click any finding and it takes you straight to the offending element, so you can judge it yourself. Maker Ján Turský says the fiddly part was teaching it when not to complain, because too many false positives make the useful findings easier to miss.
